lessons.title: Reversible reactions and dynamic equilibrium
lessons.summary: Understand what makes a reaction reversible, what dynamic equilibrium means in a closed system, and how Le Chatelier's principle predicts the effect of changing concentration, temperature and pressure.
objectives: I can describe a reversible reaction and use the ⇌ symbol correctly.
I can explain that a reversible reaction is exothermic in one direction and endothermic in the other, by the same amount of energy.
I can describe what is meant by dynamic equilibrium in a closed system.
I can use Le Chatelier's principle to predict how changing concentration, temperature or pressure shifts the position of equilibrium.

activities.title: Reversible reactions
activities.content:
## Reactions that can go backwards

Most reactions you have met so far go in one direction: burn magnesium and you get magnesium oxide, and it will not turn back into magnesium in air. But in some reactions the **products can react to re-form the reactants**. These are **reversible reactions**.

We show a reversible reaction with a double half-arrow:

$$A + B \rightleftharpoons C + D$$

The **forward reaction** goes left to right (A + B making C + D). The **reverse reaction** goes right to left (C + D making A + B).

### A classic example: ammonium chloride

When solid ammonium chloride is heated it breaks down into two gases, ammonia and hydrogen chloride. When those gases cool, they recombine to make ammonium chloride again.

$$NH_4Cl(s) \rightleftharpoons NH_3(g) + HCl(g)$$

### Another example: hydrated copper sulfate

Blue hydrated copper sulfate loses its water when heated and turns white (anhydrous copper sulfate). Add water to the white powder and it turns blue again. The direction of the reaction depends on the **conditions**, which is a big idea for this whole lesson.

activities.title: Worked example: energy in a reversible reaction
activities.content:
**Hydrated copper sulfate:**

$$CuSO_4 \cdot 5H_2O(s) \rightleftharpoons CuSO_4(s) + 5H_2O(l)$$

- The **forward** reaction (removing the water) needs heating, so it is **endothermic**.
- The **reverse** reaction (adding water back to the white powder) makes the test tube get hot, so it is **exothermic**.

The important rule: if the forward reaction is exothermic, the reverse reaction is endothermic, and **the same amount of energy is transferred in each direction**. If breaking down the hydrated salt takes in 78 kJ per mole, re-forming it releases exactly 78 kJ per mole.

**Why this matters:** later in this lesson you will predict what happens when a reaction at equilibrium is heated or cooled. To do that you must know which direction is endothermic, and this rule lets you work it out as soon as you know one direction.

question.text: The forward reaction of a reversible reaction is exothermic and releases 92 kJ per mole. Which statement about the reverse reaction is correct?
question.hint: Energy is conserved, so the energy change is the same size but in the opposite direction.
question.explanation: The reverse reaction is endothermic and takes in exactly the same amount of energy that the forward reaction releases: 92 kJ per mole.

options.text: It is endothermic and takes in 92 kJ per mole
It is exothermic and releases 92 kJ per mole
options.feedback: Both directions cannot release energy; that would create energy from nowhere.

options.text: It is endothermic and takes in less than 92 kJ per mole
Its energy change cannot be predicted

activities.title: Dynamic equilibrium
activities.content:
## What happens in a closed container?

Imagine a reversible reaction sealed in a container so that nothing can escape. This is a **closed system**.

At the start there are only reactants, so only the forward reaction can happen and it is fast. As products build up, the reverse reaction starts and gets faster, while the forward reaction slows as the reactants are used up.

Eventually the two rates become **equal**. From this point the amounts of reactants and products **stop changing**. The reaction has reached **equilibrium**.

We call it **dynamic** equilibrium because both reactions are still happening; they just cancel each other out. Picture a person walking up a downward escalator at exactly the escalator's speed: lots of movement, but no overall change in position.

### Key facts for the exam

- Equilibrium can only be reached in a **closed system** (no substances enter or leave).
- At equilibrium the **forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate**.
- The concentrations of reactants and products are **constant**, but they are **not usually equal** to each other.
- The **position of equilibrium** describes whether the mixture contains mostly products (lies to the right) or mostly reactants (lies to the left).

question.text: Which TWO statements are true about a reversible reaction at dynamic equilibrium in a closed system?
question.hint: Focus on rates rather than amounts.
question.explanation: At dynamic equilibrium both reactions continue at the same rate, so the concentrations stay constant. The concentrations of reactants and products are not necessarily equal, and the reactions have not stopped.

options.text: The forward and reverse reactions happen at the same rate
The concentrations of reactants and products remain constant
The reaction has completely stopped
options.feedback: Both reactions keep going; that is what 'dynamic' means.

options.text: The concentration of reactants equals the concentration of products
options.feedback: The amounts are constant, but they need not be equal.

activities.title: Le Chatelier's principle
activities.content:
## Predicting how equilibrium responds

If you change the conditions of a system at equilibrium, the system **responds to counteract the change**. This is **Le Chatelier's principle**, and it lets you predict which way the position of equilibrium will move (or *shift*).

There are three conditions you need to handle:

1. **Concentration** of a reactant or product.
2. **Temperature**.
3. **Pressure** (only matters for reactions involving gases).

The method is always the same:

- Ask: *what has been changed?*
- Ask: *which direction of the reaction would undo that change?*
- The equilibrium shifts in that direction until a new equilibrium is reached.

### Concentration

- **Add more of a reactant** and the equilibrium shifts to the **right** (forward) to use it up, making more product.
- **Remove a product** as it forms and the equilibrium shifts to the **right** to replace it. This trick is used in industry to keep a reaction going.
- **Add more product** and the equilibrium shifts to the **left** to remove it.

Remember that the shift happens until the concentrations settle at new constant values; the system does not return to the original amounts.

activities.title: Worked example: temperature and pressure
activities.content:
**Consider this equilibrium, where the forward reaction is exothermic:**

$$2SO_2(g) + O_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2SO_3(g)$$

**Effect of raising the temperature**

Raising the temperature adds heat. The system counteracts this by favouring the direction that **absorbs** heat: the **endothermic** direction. Here the forward reaction is exothermic, so the reverse is endothermic, and the equilibrium shifts **left**. Less SO₃ is made.

Lowering the temperature does the opposite: the exothermic (forward) direction is favoured and more SO₃ forms.

**Effect of raising the pressure**

Count the moles of gas on each side: left has 2 + 1 = **3** moles of gas, right has **2** moles. Raising the pressure makes the system favour the side with **fewer gas molecules** to reduce the pressure again. So the equilibrium shifts **right**, and more SO₃ is made.

Lowering the pressure favours the side with more gas molecules, so equilibrium shifts left.

**Watch out:** if both sides have the **same** number of gas molecules, changing the pressure has **no effect** on the position of equilibrium.

question.text: True or false: for the equilibrium $H_2(g) + I_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2HI(g)$, increasing the pressure shifts the position of equilibrium to the right.
question.hint: Count the moles of gas on each side of the equation.
question.explanation: False. There are 2 moles of gas on the left (1 + 1) and 2 moles on the right, so changing the pressure has no effect on the position of equilibrium.

options.text: True
False

activities.title: Putting it together: conditions in industry
activities.content:
## Why equilibrium matters outside the lab

Many important industrial reactions are reversible, so manufacturers use Le Chatelier's principle to squeeze out as much product as they can. But they also have to think about **rate** and **cost**, and these often pull in different directions.

Take an exothermic reaction between gases where the product side has fewer molecules.

| Change | Effect on yield (equilibrium) | Effect on rate | Practical concern |
|---|---|---|---|
| Higher pressure | Increases yield | Increases rate | Strong, expensive equipment; safety |
| Lower temperature | Increases yield | Decreases rate | Reaction may become too slow to be useful |
| Catalyst | No effect on yield | Increases rate | Reaches equilibrium faster |
| Remove product as it forms | Increases yield | – | Needs cooling or separation equipment |

A **compromise** temperature is usually chosen: high enough for a decent rate, low enough for a reasonable yield. A **catalyst** lets the reaction reach equilibrium quickly without changing where the equilibrium lies.

When you answer an industry question, say clearly whether you are talking about **yield** (how much product at equilibrium) or **rate** (how fast you get there). Mixing them up is the most common error on this topic.

question.text: Complete the sentences about a reaction at equilibrium in which the forward reaction is endothermic.

metadata.blanksText: Increasing the temperature shifts the equilibrium to the ___ because the system favours the endothermic direction. Adding a catalyst has ___ effect on the position of equilibrium but increases the ___ at which equilibrium is reached.

question.hint: The endothermic direction is the forward direction here. A catalyst changes speed, not position.
question.explanation: Heating favours the endothermic (forward) direction, so equilibrium shifts right. A catalyst has no effect on the position of equilibrium but increases the rate at which it is reached.

question.text: For the exothermic equilibrium $N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3(g)$, match each change to its effect on the position of equilibrium.
question.hint: There are 4 moles of gas on the left and 2 on the right, and the forward reaction gives out heat.
question.explanation: More pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules (right). Higher temperature favours the endothermic reverse reaction (left). Removing ammonia makes the system replace it (right). Adding a catalyst speeds both directions equally, so no shift.

pairs.right: Shifts right (fewer gas molecules on the right)
No change in position, equilibrium reached faster

question.text:
Methanol can be manufactured from carbon monoxide and hydrogen in a reversible reaction. The forward reaction is exothermic.

$$CO(g) + 2H_2(g) \rightleftharpoons CH_3OH(g)$$

(a) Explain what is meant by 'dynamic equilibrium'. (2 marks)

(b) Predict and explain the effect of increasing the pressure on the amount of methanol in the equilibrium mixture. (2 marks)
question.hint: For (a) mention both rates and concentrations. For (b) count gas molecules on each side.
question.explanation: (a) At dynamic equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions are still happening, but at the same rate, so the concentrations of reactants and products stay constant. (b) There are 3 moles of gas on the left and 1 on the right. Increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium towards the side with fewer gas molecules, the right, so more methanol is produced.

markScheme.criterion: Forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate
Concentrations / amounts of reactants and products remain constant
Equilibrium shifts to the right / more methanol is produced
Because there are fewer molecules of gas on the right-hand side

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- A **reversible reaction** can go both ways, shown by ⇌; the direction depends on the conditions.
- If one direction is **exothermic**, the other is **endothermic** by the **same** amount of energy.
- **Dynamic equilibrium** (closed system only): forward and reverse rates are **equal**, so concentrations stay **constant**.
- **Le Chatelier's principle**: the system shifts to **counteract** any change.
  - Add reactant or remove product → shifts **right**.
  - Raise temperature → favours the **endothermic** direction.
  - Raise pressure → favours the side with **fewer gas molecules**.
- A **catalyst** speeds up reaching equilibrium but does **not** change its position.

practiceQuestions.text: Which symbol is used to show a reversible reaction in a chemical equation?
practiceQuestions.hint: It has to show that the reaction can go both ways.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The double half-arrow ⇌ shows that both the forward and reverse reactions take place.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: a reversible reaction can reach equilibrium in an open beaker from which a gaseous product escapes.
practiceQuestions.hint: What kind of system is needed for equilibrium?
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. Equilibrium is only reached in a closed system. If a product escapes, the reverse reaction cannot happen and the reaction goes to completion.

options.text: True
False

practiceQuestions.text: Complete the sentence about hydrated copper sulfate.

metadata.blanksText: Heating blue hydrated copper sulfate removes water in an ___ reaction; adding water back to the white anhydrous solid is ___ and the tube becomes hot.

practiceQuestions.hint: Which direction takes in heat, and which gives it out?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Removing the water requires heating (endothermic); adding it back releases heat (exothermic).

practiceQuestions.text: Put these stages in order to describe how a reversible reaction in a sealed flask reaches equilibrium, starting with reactants only.
practiceQuestions.hint: Products have to build up before the reverse reaction can matter.
practiceQuestions.explanation: At first only the forward reaction happens. As products form the reverse reaction starts and speeds up while the forward slows. When the rates are equal, equilibrium is reached.
order: Only the forward reaction takes place and it is fast
Products build up and the reverse reaction begins
The forward reaction slows down and the reverse reaction speeds up
The two rates become equal and concentrations stop changing

practiceQuestions.text: In the equilibrium $2NO_2(g) \rightleftharpoons N_2O_4(g)$ the forward reaction is exothermic. NO₂ is brown and N₂O₄ is colourless. What happens when a sealed tube of the mixture is placed in ice-cold water?
practiceQuestions.hint: Cooling favours the direction that gives out heat.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Cooling favours the exothermic forward reaction, so more colourless N₂O₄ forms and the brown colour fades.

options.text: The mixture becomes paler because more N₂O₄ forms
The mixture becomes darker because more NO₂ forms
options.feedback: That would happen on heating, which favours the endothermic reverse reaction.

options.text: There is no change because temperature does not affect equilibrium
The reaction stops completely

practiceQuestions.text: For the equilibrium $CaCO_3(s) \rightleftharpoons CaO(s) + CO_2(g)$ in a closed container, which TWO changes would increase the amount of calcium oxide present at equilibrium? The forward reaction is endothermic.
practiceQuestions.hint: Only one side has gas, and the forward reaction takes in heat.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Increasing the temperature favours the endothermic forward direction. Removing CO₂ makes the system produce more to replace it. Increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules (left), and a catalyst does not change the position.

options.text: Increasing the temperature
Removing carbon dioxide from the container
Increasing the pressure
options.feedback: Higher pressure favours the side with less gas, which is the left.

options.text: Adding a catalyst

practiceQuestions.text: Match each term to its meaning.
practiceQuestions.hint: One is about a type of container, one about the rates, and one about which side is favoured.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A closed system lets nothing in or out; dynamic equilibrium is equal forward and reverse rates; the position of equilibrium says whether reactants or products dominate.

pairs.right: No substances can enter or leave
Forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate
Whether the mixture contains mostly reactants or mostly products

practiceQuestions.text: A student says that adding a catalyst to a reversible reaction increases the amount of product at equilibrium. Explain why the student is wrong.
practiceQuestions.hint: What does a catalyst do to the forward and reverse reactions?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions by the same amount, so equilibrium is reached faster but the position of equilibrium, and therefore the amount of product, is unchanged.

markScheme.criterion: Catalyst speeds up forward and reverse reactions equally / only affects rate
Position of equilibrium / amount of product does not change

practiceQuestions.text: In the equilibrium $N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3(g)$, how many moles of gas are there on the left-hand side of the equation?
practiceQuestions.hint: Add together the coefficients of the gases on the left.
practiceQuestions.explanation: 1 mole of N₂ + 3 moles of H₂ = 4 moles of gas.

practiceQuestions.text:
Ethanol can be made by reacting ethene with steam in a reversible reaction. The forward reaction is exothermic.

$$C_2H_4(g) + H_2O(g) \rightleftharpoons C_2H_5OH(g)$$

A manufacturer wants a high yield of ethanol but also a fast reaction. Explain why a low temperature would give a high yield but why the manufacturer chooses a moderate temperature instead. (4 marks)
practiceQuestions.hint: Link temperature to the exothermic direction for yield, and to collision theory for rate.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A low temperature favours the exothermic forward reaction, shifting the equilibrium to the right and increasing the yield of ethanol. However, at low temperature the particles have less energy so collisions are less frequent and fewer are successful, making the rate too slow. A moderate (compromise) temperature gives an acceptable yield in a reasonable time.

markScheme.criterion: Low temperature favours the exothermic / forward direction
So equilibrium shifts right / yield of ethanol increases
Low temperature makes the rate too slow / fewer successful collisions
A compromise temperature balances yield and rate
